h1: Choosing yeast for a warm room you cannot cool
title: Choosing Yeast for a Warm Room | Craft Beer School
desc: Kveik, saison and clean warm-tolerant yeasts compared, with pitching advice for rooms you cannot cool and shipping that gets hot.
teaser: If your room is 30 °C all summer, the right yeast matters more than any cooling trick. Here are the options and how to use them.
standfirst: When you cannot cool a room, change the yeast. A few families are bred for heat. This guide explains what each does and how to pitch it.
sections: The problem with the usual ale yeast

Most standard ale yeasts are happiest between 18 and 22 °C. Above that they throw more fruity esters and fusel alcohols and at the extreme they can stall. If the beer is also several degrees above room temperature during active fermentation, a 28 °C room can mean a 32 °C ferment.

Kveik is a family of yeast from Norwegian farmhouse brewing, kept alive for generations by drying and passing on. Many strains ferment cleanly in the 30s °C and finish a beer in two to four days. They also tolerate high alcohol. Flavour varies by strain: some are neutral, others make citrus or stone-fruit esters that suit pale ales. Dried kveik is now widely available and travels well.

Pitch a normal amount, ferment at 30 to 35 °C if you wish and expect a vigorous start. Use a blow-off tube. Taste your first batch before assuming a strain is neutral.

Saison strains are classic Belgian farmhouse yeasts that like it hot, often 25 to 32 °C. They make peppery, fruity, dry beers. Some stall if they are kept cool, so let the temperature rise as fermentation slows. They suit a hot room well, but they ferment very dry. Mash a bit higher than usual if you want some body.
Clean warm-tolerant ale and lager strains

Several dry ale strains and some dry lager strains, sold as tolerant of the high teens °C, make clean beer if you can keep them out of the high 20s. They are the best choice if you only need to bridge a gap of a few degrees. Read the supplier's stated range, then add a safety margin.

Dry yeast survives heat better than liquid. If a liquid yeast arrived warm, see reviving liquid yeast that arrived warm. Keep dry yeast sachets in the fridge when possible, but a few weeks at room temperature will not ruin them.

Rehydrate according to the pack. Pitch into cool wort, below 25 °C if you can. Then let fermentation warm itself up. Underpitching in heat makes things worse. A bigger pitch ferments faster, which gets the beer through the risky early hours.
A test batch before the big one

Run a small experiment. Brew a simple 5 L pale beer, split it into two 2.5 L jars and pitch a different yeast in each. Ferment both in the same spot, log the beer temperature daily and taste side by side at bottling and again three weeks later. It costs two sachets and an afternoon and the answer is specific to your room.

Write down the temperature curve. Many first-time warm brewers are surprised by how fast the beer heats in the first 48 hours and how little the room seems to matter after that. A yeast that behaves well on your curve is the right one for you.

Also taste for the standard faults: banana and nail polish for heat stress, butter for rushed finishing, a sour edge for infection. A cheesy or dull aroma points to stale hops rather than the yeast (see hop freshness across long supply chains).

A yeast packet states a temperature range, an attenuation (how much sugar the yeast eats, as a percentage) and a flocculation (how fast it settles). For a warm room, look first at the top of the temperature range, then at attenuation. High attenuation, above about 80 per cent, gives a dry beer, which suits hot weather. Low flocculation leaves a hazy beer, which is fine for some styles and a nuisance for others.

Treat the stated range as the supplier's best case. Brew within it with a margin of two or three degrees below the top.

Warm yeasts suit pale ales, saisons, wheat beers and fruit beers. They are not good for delicate pilsner-style beers. For lager-style approaches, see fermenting a lager-style beer without a fridge.

Whichever yeast you choose, keep the first few batches simple and record temperatures. The yeast will teach you more than any chart. If your grist uses local grains, sorghum and cassava in commercial brewing covers the cooking and yeast nutrition they need.

Understanding what yeast needs (oxygen, nutrients, healthy cells, the right pitch) is the foundation of all good brewing and it is where we start in class.
faqs: Kveik strains and many saison yeasts are suited to it. Standard ale yeasts are not and will give harsh flavours.
Many strains are, even at 35 °C. Some give fruity esters. Check the strain description and try a small batch.
Does dry yeast survive a hot journey?
Usually yes. Dry yeast is far more robust than liquid in warm shipping.
Should I pitch more yeast in a warm room?
A healthy, full pitch helps because fermentation starts quickly and stays clean. Underpitched warm ferments are the worst.
